analysis.one_liner: Sets enforceable rights for people in HMOs, from emergency care to outside appeals of denied treatment.
analysis.headline: The patient bill of rights won 24 Democratic cosponsors but was referred to two House committees in October 1997 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written a bill of rights for people enrolled in managed care (HMO-type) plans: guaranteed coverage of medically necessary care, direct access to an obstetrician-gynecologist, emergency room coverage without prior approval, a ban on paying doctors to limit care, a ban on "gag" clauses restricting what doctors can tell patients, and outside appeals when care is denied. It also would have let patients sue their health plan in state court for injuries or wrongful death, which federal law largely blocked at the time. It applied both to private group plans under ERISA and to plans regulated by the Public Health Service Act, and it let states keep stricter protections.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans. They would get guaranteed coverage of medically necessary treatment, second opinions paid even from out-of-network doctors, a choice of at least three providers they could switch at any time, continued treatment when the plan drops a provider, direct access to an OB-GYN without a referral, emergency care covered under a "prudent layperson" standard without prior authorization, ongoing specialist referrals for chronic conditions, trained medical interpreters where at least 2% of enrollees need them, protection from retaliation for filing complaints, external independent review of denied care with the plan paying the cost, and the right to sue the plan in state court for personal injury or wrongful death.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients enrolled in HMO and managed care plans

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees coverage of emergency services no matter which hospital treats the patient and without prior authorization, using a 'prudent layperson' standard so coverage turns on the patient's symptoms, not the final diagnosis.

Bars managed care plans from offering doctors financial incentives to reduce or limit medically necessary care, and voids contract 'gag clauses' that stop doctors from discussing treatment options or the plan's financial incentives with patients.

Lets women designate an obstetrician-gynecologist as their primary care provider, or get routine gynecological and pregnancy care without their primary doctor's prior approval, and requires plans to cover treatment by a nonparticipating specialist at in-network rates when the plan itself makes the referral.

Creates a grievance process, protects patients and doctors from reprisal for using it, and adds an external review by an independent state-certified organization after internal appeals are exhausted, with the plan — not the patient — bearing the cost.

Overrides the part of ERISA that preempted state lawsuits, letting patients bring state-court claims for personal injury or wrongful death against the people providing insurance or administrative services to their health plan — the main practical remedy for a wrongly denied treatment.

Requires plans in areas with medically underserved populations to file an access plan, provides trained interpreters and bilingual information where at least 2% of enrollees need them, and prohibits discrimination based on health status, age, language, income, or expected need for services.

analysis.who_pays: Managed care plans and the employers that sponsor group coverage would bear the cost: compliance with network-adequacy rules (including at least one primary care doctor per 1,500 enrollees and a choice of at least three providers in each category), interpreter services, external review expenses, and exposure to state-court damage suits. Some of those costs would be passed back to workers and consumers as higher premiums; the bill did not include federal funding to offset them.
analysis.who_pays_short: HMOs, insurers, and employers sponsoring plans

drawbacks.text: The mandates are broad and unfunded: plans would have to meet specific network ratios (one primary care physician per 1,500 enrollees), offer at least three provider choices in every category, fund interpreters, and pay for external review, and much of that cost would likely show up as higher premiums for employers and workers.

Section 4 opens health plans to state damage suits for personal injury and wrongful death, which would add litigation exposure and could further raise premiums — the tradeoff an honest supporter would have to acknowledge against the remedy it gives injured patients.

Federal rules would preempt nothing but set a floor, and the bill lets states go further; a small plan serving a dispersed rural area could find the fixed network and choice requirements hard to meet without consolidation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections target documented managed care practices that harmed patients — paying doctors to limit care, gag clauses, denied emergency visits, blocked lawsuits — and the remedies are concrete and enforceable. The costs are real but ordinary for health regulation: higher premiums and litigation exposure, and the bill chose broad federal mandates over a more targeted design, which is why industry and employer opposition was certain to be heavy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees in October 1997 and then to their health subcommittees, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on October 2, 1997, with 21 original cosponsors; it was referred to both the Commerce Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee.
Within three weeks it was sent to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care plans, insurers, and employers that sponsor health benefits came out ahead: they avoided federal coverage mandates, external review costs, and state-court liability, while patients in HMOs gained no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: HMOs, insurers, and employers that fund plans

for.name: Nydia Velazquez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Managed Care Bill of Rights for Consumers Act of 1997 and recruited the bill's cosponsors.

for.name: 24 of 207 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 24 cosponsors were Democrats, including House Minority Whip David Bonior and Reps. Conyers, Rangel, Lowey, Schumer, and Slaughter.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out or scheduled a markup; the bill's last action was a subcommittee referral.

against.name: William F. Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Second committee of referral; likewise took no action beyond sending the bill to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee.

against.name: HMO and health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public campaign in 1997-1998 against federal managed care mandates and liability expansion, arguing they would raise premiums.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-controlled committees never acted, so the bill never reached a floor vote where the partisan split could be tested.

industries.note: The bill bans the plan practices that generated the managed care backlash — financial incentives for doctors to limit care, gag clauses, narrow referral and emergency-coverage rules — and adds independent external review plus state-court liability. Plans would lose pricing and utilization-control discretion and bear direct compliance and litigation costs.

ERISA-covered group plans would have to meet the same patient protections, raising benefit costs; the bill phases in collective bargaining contracts at their expiration dates in recognition of that burden. Workers gain protections, but some cost would return to them as premiums.

industries.industry: Trial lawyers and personal injury plaintiffs
industries.note: Section 4 creates a state cause of action for personal injury or wrongful death against health plan service providers, restoring a legal remedy that ERISA preemption had largely closed off. Patients injured by denied care gain the same access to the courts.

Doctors gain bans on gag clauses and on incentives to limit care, protection from reprisal, and guaranteed continuity for patients when a plan drops them; plans face requirements to maintain adequate networks, which would support provider participation.
